# Results — Study 361 (Zweig Breadth Thrust)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Marty Zweig's **Breadth
Thrust** — the rare "all-clear" buy signal said to be "never wrong" — tested on a
**transparent breadth proxy**. True NYSE advance/decline breadth is not free on yfinance, so
we construct the breadth from a fixed 40-name large-cap basket: each day's advance ratio is
**advancers / (advancers + decliners)** across the basket. A thrust fires when the 10-day EMA
of that ratio climbs from below **0.40** to above **0.615** within ~10 trading days. We then
measure forward 3/6/12-month SPY returns after each thrust vs the unconditional base rate.
Offline & deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — SPY + a fixed 40-name large-cap basket (public, no key) |
| Window | 1995-01-04 → 2026-06-22 (**7,918** trading days; **31.5** years) |
| Breadth proxy | fraction of basket advancing each day; **PROXY** for NYSE (adv issues / total issues) |
| Thrust rule | 10-day EMA of adv-ratio crosses **0.40 → 0.615** within 10 trading days (Zweig) |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag; one round-trip cost of 5 bps on a buy-and-hold trade |

> **Proxy caveat (named on the Signal axis).** A 40-name surviving-large-cap basket is a
> *noisier, narrower* breadth gauge than the ~3,000-issue NYSE Zweig used, and it carries
> **survivorship** (breadth-of-the-survivors runs mildly bullish). Our proxy fires **22**
> times in 31.5 years — looser than the canonical "~a dozen ever" because a small basket
> swings past 0.40/0.615 more easily. The verdict does **not** hinge on the proxy's exact
> count: it hinges on the fact that *any* ~once-a-year-or-rarer signal is statistically
> underpowered, which holds a fortiori for the true ~once-a-decade NYSE thrust.

## The signal — forward SPY returns after a thrust vs the base rate

1-day entry lag; the unconditional column is *all* overlapping forward windows over the same
tape (the honest base rate). Welch *t* compares the conditional mean to the unconditional
mean; the placebo *p* is the share of 20,000 random same-size date draws whose mean forward
return **beats** the thrust set.

| horizon | n thrusts | cond. mean | cond. win-rate | base mean | base win-rate | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 3-month  | 22 | **+2.37%** | 59% | +2.93% | 71% | **−0.37** | 0.644 |
| 6-month  | 22 | **+6.18%** | 73% | +5.89% | 76% | **+0.13** | 0.461 |
| 12-month | 22 | **+14.99%** | **91%** | +12.01% | 81% | **+0.94** | 0.207 |

Read it carefully. The famous **"never wrong"** headline lives in the **12-month win-rate**:
after a thrust SPY is higher a year later **91%** of the time. But the unconditional 12-month
win-rate is already **81%** — the US tape rises most years anyway. The *excess* mean return is
only ~3 points, and at **t = 0.94 / placebo p = 0.21** it is **statistically
indistinguishable from drawing 22 random dates**. Worse, at **3 months the conditional mean is
*below* the base rate** (t = −0.37): the effect **flips sign** with horizon. There is no robust
edge here — there is a small, noisy, horizon-dependent number measured on **22 events**.

## Costs barely matter — which is itself the point

| horizon | n trades | gross mean | net @ 5 bps round-trip |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 3-month  | 22 | +2.37% | +2.32% |
| 6-month  | 22 | +6.18% | +6.13% |
| 12-month | 22 | +14.99% | +14.94% |

A 5 bps round-trip shaves essentially nothing off a multi-month hold — costs are **not** the
problem. The problem is **frequency**: **22 trades in 31.5 years (≈ one every 1.4 years)**
cannot be a NAV-scale strategy. You cannot allocate capital to a rule that signals you in once
a year, and the true NYSE thrust signals **once a decade**. The edge, even if it were real,
is undeployable.

## Robustness — the result is flat in the threshold

| upper threshold | n events | cond. 12m mean | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.610 | 22 | +15.1% | 0.99 | 0.197 |
| **0.615** (Zweig) | 22 | +15.0% | 0.94 | 0.207 |
| 0.650 | 15 | +15.5% | 0.68 | 0.220 |

Tightening to 0.65 (closer to the canonical "dozen" count of 15) only *lowers* the *t* — fewer
events, weaker test. There is no threshold at which the signal clears t = 2.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, and small samples are weak

On a deterministic breadth series with **12 thrusts injected by construction** and a SPY-like
price, the detector finds the injected events and the inference behaves exactly as it should:

| planted 6-month edge | detected | cond. 6m mean | base 6m mean | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no edge) | 15 | +8.84% | +4.98% | 1.19 | 0.093 |
| **+0.10** (large edge) | 15 | +17.30% | +7.38% | **3.18** | **0.001** |

With **no** planted edge the test does **not** cross t = 2 (it cannot manufacture significance
from ~a dozen events, even when noise tilts the point estimate up). Only a **huge** planted
edge — +10% over six months — drives t to 3.2. The control proves two things at once: the
measurement engine is unbiased, **and** ~a dozen events is too few to detect any edge of
plausible magnitude. That is the entire lesson.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The folklore is partly real: the 12-month win-rate after a thrust is high
  (**91%**), and the conditional mean is positive at 6/12 months. But the *excess* over the
  unconditional base rate is small, **fails the t ≥ 2 bar** (t = 0.94, placebo p = 0.21), and
  **flips sign at 3 months**. Literature support + a positive-but-insignificant point estimate
  ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Costs are negligible, but the rule fires **~22 times in 31 years**
  (the true NYSE version: ~once a decade). A signal you can act on under once a year, whose
  excess return is inside the noise, is **not a NAV-scale strategy**.
- **"Never wrong"? — BUSTED.** The "never-wrong" reputation is a **sample-size + base-rate
  illusion**: with a dozen-ish occurrences in a market that rises most years anyway, a high
  win-rate is what you'd expect by luck. It is **Study 167 (Hindenburg-Omen) inverted** — there
  a rare signal "always" precedes crashes; here a rare signal "always" precedes rallies. Both
  are the same statistical mirage wearing opposite costumes.
